Wood Dale sits in DuPage County, part of the broader Chicago-area O'Hare-adjacent data center corridor that has drawn colocation and enterprise demand for its proximity to the airport, fiber density, and access to ComEd power infrastructure, alongside other operators tracked elsewhere in this registry. No independent trade-press coverage distinguishing CH1 from CH2 in construction date or expansion history was located this session.

profile.reading:
This building at 8025 North Interstate Highway 35, on a service road on Austin's north side in Travis County, is a standalone colocation data center Element Critical brands as its Austin One facility. Element Critical is a privately held US colocation operator backed by the investment firms Safanad and Industry Capital, running a small portfolio concentrated in Texas, including this site and a facility in Houston. The building predates Element Critical's ownership. Digital Realty Trust developed and owned it before selling it in August 2017 to vXchnge, a colocation provider, for a reported 20 million dollars, according to trade press coverage of that sale. vXchnge ran the property for about four years before Element Critical bought it, a transaction announced in September 2021 and described in press coverage as Element Critical's second Texas data center. The purchase price was not disclosed.

Element Critical's own materials describe Austin One as a 62,300 square foot standalone building on a seven acre private campus, built to Tier III, concurrently maintainable standards, with six distinct utility feeds and cold aisle containment cooling. Two of the operator's own published documents give slightly different power figures for the same building. The main Element Critical website states 9.5 megawatts of total utility power. The operator's own facility brochure for this address instead states 7 megawatts of total capacity paired with 8.5 megawatts of N plus one generator backup power, configurable to 2N, and describes room to expand to 13 megawatts. Read together, these figures are consistent with roughly 7 megawatts of current IT critical load, a figure matched by trade press describing the same number as critical load capacity at the time of the 2021 sale, sitting under a larger utility feed and an oversized N plus one diesel plant. No source found reconciles the 9.5 and 7 megawatt figures directly, so both are recorded here as operator published rather than treated as a single settled number. The facility holds SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, and ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certifications, states PCI DSS and HIPAA/HITECH compliance, and reported more than ten on site carriers and roughly sixty enterprise customers around the time of the 2021 sale.

No zoning case, tax abatement agreement, or contested public hearing tied specifically to this address turned up in a search of Austin and Travis County public records, consistent with a history of ownership changing hands on an existing building rather than new construction requiring rezoning or site plan review. The building does sit inside a city now actively writing new rules for the industry as a category. In August 2026, Austin City Council began work on a dedicated data center zoning classification, water, noise, and lighting standards, and a formal statement that the city will not incentivize data center construction, reporting from the Texas Tribune shows, with Council Member Ryan Alter seeking authority to deny future projects and Council Member Vanessa Fuentes favoring a moratorium. That same reporting states Austin Energy currently serves about ten existing data centers drawing between one and twenty megawatts each, a bracket this facility's own disclosed numbers fall within, while the state's regulatory definition of a large load user begins at 75 megawatts, a threshold well beyond this building's scale. Travis Central Appraisal District's parcel records were not successfully queried in this research session, so the assessed value and county of record owner are not confirmed here beyond the operator's own public statements.

profile.reading:
The registry maps this row as Element Critical VA1 at 7980 Quantum Drive in the Tysons area of Vienna, Fairfax County, Virginia, roughly 500 metres from the site of the original MAE East internet exchange that made this corner of Northern Virginia a network crossroads in the 1990s. The address needs a caveat. OpenStreetMap tags the mapped building as 7980 Quantum Drive, while Element Critical's own entry in PeeringDB gives its Northern Virginia VA1 facility as 7990 Quantum Drive, Vienna, Virginia 22182, under the alternate legal name Tysons Enterprise DC, LLC, with FiberLight listed as a carrier and a property note reading Diverse Serving Substations. The two coordinate sets sit about seventy metres apart, and 7980 and 7990 are adjacent buildings on the same fourteen and a half acre assemblage, so the registry point is on the right block even if the door number is uncertain.

Element Critical is a privately held colocation operator that rebranded from Central Colo in 2017. Its current website lists only Austin, Houston and Chicago, with no Virginia site, which is consistent with an exit rather than an omission. Trade press reports that Serverfarm bought 7980 and 7990 Quantum Drive from Legacy Investing and Element Critical in October 2025. The chain of title before that runs from SAIC, which sold in 2011 to the Meridian Group for 63 million dollars, to Element Critical and Legacy for 97 million dollars in 2017. A 2019 announcement from Phillips Realty Capital adds that EagleBank lent 67 million dollars against 7990 Quantum Drive on 26 August 2019, a 199,097 square foot building constructed in 1978, to fund roughly 130,000 square feet of raised floor and an 8 megawatt critical power expansion in N plus 1 configuration.

Power here has to be read carefully. An older Element Critical brochure, quoted in trade press, describes 10 megawatts of utility power across 87,560 square feet of raised floor with headroom to 15 megawatts. That is the electrical service available to the building, not IT load, and it should never be reprinted as capacity. The only IT side number in the public record is the 8 megawatts of critical power the 2019 financing was raised to install, and that is a lender side description of planned work rather than a measured operating load. No standby diesel rating was published for the Element Critical era, and no current operating IT load is published at all, so none is stored.

The local record is where this site becomes worth reading. On 10 September 2024 the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors adopted a data centre zoning ordinance amendment requiring buildings to stand at least 200 feet from a residential lot line, equipment such as backup generators to stand 300 feet away or be shielded by the building itself, a minimum distance of one mile from a Metro station, screening or enclosure of all equipment, and both pre construction and post construction noise studies. Serverfarm's redevelopment, filed as the Vienna Cloud project, needs relief on several of those points at once. Fairfax County accepted the proffered condition amendment and special exception, case REC26-00000-008C7, on 4 May 2026, with a Planning Commission public hearing set for 18 November 2026. The application covers 14.4 acres and two buildings totalling roughly 316,228 square feet, taking 7980 Quantum from 80,256 to 95,014 square feet and 7990 Quantum from 202,500 to 221,214 square feet, at a maximum height of 67 feet, with floor area ratio raised from 0.40 to 0.50. The site sits 0.9 miles from the Tysons Corner Metro entrance, inside the one mile exclusion. Setbacks to the Reserve at Tysons Corner apartments and the Heritage Point townhouses would be 107 to 131 feet rather than 200. Twenty eight diesel generators would sit in a yard at the rear of the property, and the applicant states that fully enclosing them is not mechanically feasible. Against that the filing offers a five foot off site sidewalk on Kidwell Drive, a public playground, an art wall on the screening structure, and about thirty fewer trees than the canopy standard would normally require, and projects 29 weekday morning peak trips against the 157 already approved for the offices. Renee Grebe of Nature Forward has objected on noise grounds, describing twenty four hours a day of it beside homes and a sports field.

What is not known is whether any colocation is still operating in the building today, what its present IT load is, and what Fairfax County staff will recommend, since no staff report had been published when this entry was written.

reading:
Element Critical is a privately held colocation operator whose two Illinois buildings in this registry have a clear paper trail, because they changed hands in a transaction both parties described. In January 2019 Element Critical bought two Chicago area data centres from Sungard Availability Services, the disaster recovery specialist, in a deal reported at 195,000 square feet combined with 111,000 square feet of raised floor and up to 15 MW. The purchase price was not disclosed, but Element Critical committed about $40 million to upgrade and expand the two properties. They sit roughly 1,000 feet apart in Wood Dale, about 17 miles west of downtown Chicago and around two miles from O'Hare International Airport.

The operator publishes specifications for both. Chicago One, at 711 North Edgewood Avenue, is 151,000 square feet with 85,500 square feet of raised floor and 7 MW available in N, N+1 and 2N configurations, fed from dual substations by diverse pathways, cooled by air cooled chillers at N+20 percent unit redundancy, supporting air cooled densities from 2 kW to 20 kW per rack with liquid immersion options, and carrying seven on net providers. Chicago Two, at 341 Haynes Drive, is 45,000 square feet with 26,000 square feet of raised floor and 5 MW of total utility power, again from dual substations, with the same cooling approach and density range and eight providers on net. Both hold SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type 2 attestations, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS, and are described as HIPAA compliant.

Those megawatt figures are worth naming precisely. Chicago One's 7 MW is described as power available in configurable redundancy, and Chicago Two's 5 MW is described as total utility power. Neither is a stated critical IT load. Separately, the company markets scalable deployments up to 50 MW across its platform, which is a sales ceiling for prospective customers rather than built capacity at any named building.

The corporate wrapper changed recently. On 18 December 2025 Element Critical announced a relaunched United States data centre platform backed by Mercuria, 26North, Arctos and Safanad, with Ken Parent as chief executive, anchored on two newly acquired enterprise data centres in Houston and Austin alongside the existing Chicago operations, and positioned around AI inference demand for enterprise, financial services, healthcare and energy customers. The announcement names no capacity figure and no dollar commitment, and the company's own About page states no headquarters address or founding year, so this registry leaves headquarters unrecorded rather than inferring one from its market list.
